analysis.one_liner: Halts construction of large AI data centers until Congress passes laws on AI safety, jobs, utility bills, and community approval.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 25, 2026, the bill has no cosponsors and sits in the Senate Commerce Committee with no further action or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would block any new or expanded AI data center — large computing facilities that power AI, which now drive a big share of new electricity demand — until Congress passes laws requiring federal review of AI products before release, protections against AI-driven job loss and sharing of AI wealth, plus rules that data centers must not raise consumers' utility bills, must protect the environment, must win local community approval, must create union jobs, and may receive no government subsidies. It also would bar exporting AI computing hardware to countries without comparable laws, and require the Energy Department to publish quarterly reports on data centers' financing, energy and water use, emissions, noise, and wages. As of now it has taken no further step than being sent to a Senate committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households and workers gain if the bill passes: their electricity bills are shielded from data-center-driven rate increases, their communities get veto power over new facilities, water and emissions get public reporting, and future AI gains are directed toward workers rather than only tech shareholders. Employees threatened by AI-driven job displacement benefit from the required anti-displacement policies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households facing rising power bills and AI job displacement

how_it_helps.text: It stops construction and upgrades of AI data centers (generally those over 20 megawatts or using high-power/liquid-cooled racks) until Congress enacts laws requiring federal pre-release approval of AI products and ensuring AI's economic gains benefit workers, not just tech company owners.

Any future data centers must, under those laws, not raise consumers' utility bills, not harm the climate or environment, win approval from affected communities, create union jobs with prevailing wages and apprenticeships, and receive no government subsidies.

The Department of Energy must publish quarterly reports on each AI data center's financing, water and energy use, emissions, noise, wages, and jobs — giving the public information that companies now generally do not disclose.
It bans exports of AI computing hardware to any country without comparable safeguards, aiming to keep foreign-built AI data centers from simply replacing the ones blocked here.

analysis.who_pays: AI companies and cloud providers pay by halting data center buildouts; semiconductor exporters lose foreign sales; local governments that court data centers for tax revenue and construction jobs forgo them during the moratorium; construction and trade unions forgo near-term work the projects would have created.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big Tech, chip exporters, and data center developers

drawbacks.text: The moratorium would halt construction and upgrades of AI data centers of any size above the bill's thresholds with no time limit, potentially slowing AI capabilities, services, and the construction jobs and local tax revenue that come with data center projects.

The trigger for lifting the moratorium requires Congress to pass laws imposing federal pre-release review of AI products and wealth-sharing policies — an unusually high bar that gives an individual senator's moratorium leverage over unrelated future legislation.

The export ban on AI computing hardware to any country without comparable laws would hit US semiconductor makers' foreign sales and could push other countries to build their own AI hardware supply chains outside US reach.

Preventing any increase in consumers' utility bills is hard to guarantee by law, and a blanket ban on subsidies for data centers would go well beyond what many state and local governments now offer to attract them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real and growing cost to ordinary people: AI data centers are raising electricity prices, straining water supplies, and are routinely subsidized with public money while the AI gains flow to a handful of tech companies and their owners. But the design is a very heavy instrument. A construction halt until Congress passes sweeping AI laws — including federal pre-release approval of AI products — is a much bigger ask than a permitting or rate-review bill, gives AI rivals abroad a wide opening during the pause, and the export ban would invite retaliation against the semiconductor and cloud industries. A narrower bill targeting the subsidies, utility-bill cost shifts, and community veto alone would likely face less resistance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat since March 2026 with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote.

narrative.text: Introduced March 25, 2026, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, the standard first step for a Senate bill.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill has support only from its author, Senator Sanders.
Since that referral, no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — has been recorded, and the moratorium it proposes is not in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: AI companies and utilities planning large data center buildouts, since nothing has been built differently; no one else's situation has changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: AI companies and data center builders

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, citing warnings from AI executives and researchers about job displacement, energy and water strains, and existential risk, and referred it to committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no other senator has joined, so the bill's partisan shape is simply that its sole supporter is an Independent known for challenging corporate power.

industries.industry: Big Tech / AI companies (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, xAI)
industries.note: Their buildout of large AI data centers would stop at the border of the moratorium, which cannot lift until Congress passes sweeping AI safety, job-protection, and wealth-sharing laws. They would also face quarterly public reporting on their data centers' finances, energy, water, emissions, and labor practices.

The bill takes aim at the data-center-driven growth in electricity demand that is raising rates for households; future centers must demonstrably not increase consumers' utility bills. Utilities' large data-center customers face new scrutiny and community veto power.

industries.industry: Semiconductor makers (Nvidia, AMD, and chip equipment makers)
industries.note: The export ban would bar them from selling AI computing hardware to any country without comparable AI laws, cutting off foreign customers that now drive much of their revenue.

industries.industry: Data center construction, real estate, and cloud infrastructure
industries.note: New AI data center projects and expansions would be frozen; the bill would also bar government subsidies for any future AI data centers, removing a revenue stream many projects rely on.

Any post-moratorium centers would have to create union jobs with prevailing wages and apprenticeships, a gain for organized labor, though the moratorium itself halts the projects that would create those jobs.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action months after introduction, the bill is effectively dead for this Congress. Similar sweeping AI moratorium proposals have not advanced, and the Commerce Committee is unlikely to schedule a hearing on a construction ban opposed by the tech industry; the bill's realistic value is as a statement of position heading into elections.
